pharm: Short-acting ester local anesthetic that reversibly blocks neuronal voltage-gated sodium channels, preventing nerve impulse initiation and conduction to produce local/regional anesthesia.
quick: Infiltration/peripheral nerve block: total dose individualized, typically up to 800 mg (11 mg/kg) without epinephrine
Used in obstetric regional anesthesia; use as clinically indicated
Short-acting; brief interruption generally unnecessary, use clinical judgment
Use with caution; little change as it is rapidly metabolized in plasma
Metabolized by plasma esterases, not the liver; little hepatic impact
Not directly relevant; avoid additive CNS depression with sedatives
Cardiovascular and respiratory status, signs of systemic toxicity (LAST)
summary: Chloroprocaine is a rapid-onset, short-acting ester-type local anesthetic used for infiltration anesthesia, peripheral nerve block, and epidural (including caudal) anesthesia, including in obstetrics. It is rapidly hydrolyzed by plasma pseudocholinesterase, giving a very short systemic half-life and a wide safety margin for systemic toxicity. The principal serious hazards are local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) - CNS excitation/seizures progressing to depression, and cardiovascular collapse - and, with neuraxial use, hypotension and high/total spinal block. As an ester, it carries a risk of hypersensitivity reactions (related to PABA metabolites).
indications: Production of local anesthesia by infiltration and peripheral nerve block
Epidural and caudal anesthesia, including for surgical and obstetric procedures

dosage.d: 1-2% solution; individualize to the smallest effective dose

dosage.n: Epinephrine prolongs effect and reduces peak levels

dosage.d: Maximum 11 mg/kg; use lower concentrations and individualized dosing

admin: Administer only by clinicians experienced in regional anesthesia, with resuscitation equipment and drugs immediately available
Aspirate before and during injection to avoid intravascular or intrathecal injection; use incremental dosing
Use a test dose where appropriate for epidural/caudal techniques
Use the lowest dose and concentration that produces the desired effect
Do not use solutions containing preservatives (e.g., methylparaben) for spinal or epidural anesthesia
moa: Chloroprocaine is an amino-ester local anesthetic. It diffuses across the nerve cell membrane in its uncharged base form and, in its ionized form, binds the intracellular portion of voltage-gated sodium channels. By blocking sodium influx, it inhibits the depolarization needed to initiate and propagate action potentials, thereby reversibly blocking nerve conduction. Smaller, myelinated, and more rapidly firing fibers (pain and autonomic) are blocked before larger motor fibers. Its very rapid onset reflects its physicochemical properties, and its short duration reflects extremely rapid hydrolysis by plasma pseudocholinesterase.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to chloroprocaine or other ester-type local anesthetics (or to PABA/para-aminobenzoic acid derivatives)
Hypersensitivity to any component of the formulation
relative: Contraindications to the specific regional technique (e.g., infection at injection site, coagulopathy for neuraxial block, increased intracranial pressure)
Severe hemorrhage, hypotension, or shock (for neuraxial techniques)
Pre-existing CNS or cardiac conduction disease
Severe hepatic or renal impairment (general caution)
monitor: Cardiovascular status (blood pressure, heart rate, ECG)
Level/spread of anesthetic block and consciousness
Early signs of systemic toxicity (perioral numbness, tinnitus, restlessness)

preg: Chloroprocaine is used in obstetric anesthesia (epidural/caudal); its very rapid maternal metabolism limits fetal exposure. Use as clinically indicated, observing techniques to avoid maternal hypotension and fetal compromise; avoid paracervical block in situations of fetal distress.
lact: Chloroprocaine is very short-acting and rapidly metabolized; the amount appearing in breast milk after appropriate use is expected to be minimal, and breastfeeding can generally continue. Use clinical judgment.
renal: Chloroprocaine is metabolized in plasma rather than excreted unchanged by the kidneys, so renal impairment has little direct effect on its clearance; nevertheless, use general caution in significant renal impairment.
hepatic: Chloroprocaine is metabolized by plasma pseudocholinesterase rather than hepatic enzymes, so hepatic impairment has little effect on its metabolism. General caution is advised in severely debilitated patients.

major: Other local anesthetics or antiarrhythmics (e.g., lidocaine, mexiletine) - additive systemic and cardiac toxicity
Drugs that depress cardiac conduction/contractility - additive cardiovascular depression with regional block
moderate: MAO inhibitors and tricyclic antidepressants - increased risk of hypertension when local anesthetic solutions contain epinephrine
Ergot-type oxytocics - severe persistent hypertension with epinephrine-containing solutions
Sulfonamides - the PABA metabolite of chloroprocaine can antagonize sulfonamide activity
Cholinesterase inhibitors / drugs reducing plasma cholinesterase - prolonged chloroprocaine effect
minor: CNS depressants - additive sedation if systemic absorption occurs
interactions.alcohol: No direct interaction; avoid additive CNS/respiratory depression with sedatives.
interactions.diagnostics: Its metabolite (para-aminobenzoic acid, PABA) can interfere with the action of sulfonamide antibacterials.

serious: Local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) - CNS excitation/seizures then depression
High or total spinal block with respiratory paralysis
rare: Neurological injury / persistent sensory or motor deficit after neuraxial use
Cauda equina syndrome (with inadvertent high-concentration intrathecal exposure historically)
emergency: Seizures progressing to coma and respiratory arrest

monitoring: Continuous cardiovascular monitoring (blood pressure, heart rate, ECG) during and after administration
Level and spread of the anesthetic block and patient consciousness
Watch for early symptoms of systemic toxicity (circumoral numbness, tinnitus, lightheadedness, agitation)
counsel: This anesthetic is given by your clinician for a procedure; it numbs a specific area and wears off quickly
Tell your anesthetist about any previous reaction to a local anesthetic or 'caine' drugs
Numbness, tingling, or weakness in the treated area is expected and should resolve as the medicine wears off
Report immediately any ringing in the ears, metallic taste, dizziness, restlessness, or twitching during injection
After a nerve block, protect the numb area from injury until sensation fully returns
pk: Very rapid - typically within 6-12 minutes for regional anesthesia
Plasma levels and block establish within minutes of injection
Extremely short - approximately 21-25 seconds (adult plasma); rapidly hydrolyzed by plasma esterases
Store at 20-25 C (excursions 15-30 C permitted); protect from light; do not use discolored solutions
pearls: Ester-type local anesthetic - rapidly hydrolyzed by plasma pseudocholinesterase, giving very short duration and a wide systemic safety margin
Local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) is the key danger - have lipid emulsion (Intralipid) and resuscitation ready; treat seizures and cardiovascular collapse promptly
Aspirate and use incremental dosing to avoid intravascular or intrathecal injection
Its PABA metabolite can cause ester-class allergy and can antagonize sulfonamide antibiotics
Preservative-containing formulations must not be used for spinal/epidural anesthesia
missed: Not applicable - chloroprocaine is administered as a single procedure by a clinician and has no chronic dosing schedule.
overdose: Overdose or inadvertent intravascular injection causes local anesthetic systemic toxicity: CNS excitation (restlessness, tinnitus, perioral numbness, seizures) followed by CNS depression, and cardiovascular toxicity (hypotension, arrhythmias, cardiac arrest). Management: stop injection, secure airway and give oxygen/ventilation, control seizures (benzodiazepines), support circulation, and administer intravenous lipid emulsion (lipid rescue) for severe cardiovascular toxicity; provide advanced cardiac life support as needed.
